move: Give people a reason to come on your slowest day: one recurring event at a fixed time, every week, such as a tasting, a quiz, a supper club or a live set.
why: A recurring event brings people who were not coming at all, where a discount mostly moves regulars who would have paid full price.
example: 15 extra covers at $30 a head is $450 a week, about $23,400 over a year.
watch: Run it 6 weeks before you judge it, and keep the night fixed. A recurring event that skips weeks never builds a habit.
follow_up: What event would suit my room?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Before you discount a slow day, add something worth coming for: a dish or offer you only serve that day, at full price.
why: A blanket discount cuts margin on every cover, including the regulars who would have come anyway.
example: 20% off a $30 check gives away $6 a cover, so 40 covers costs you $240 before it brings anyone new.
watch: If you do discount, cap it to one item or one hour, and count new faces, not total covers.
follow_up: What should I serve on my slow day?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Prep your 5 best sellers to the edge before the rush and put your fastest people on the stations that sell them.
why: In a rush most tickets are the same few items, so speed there is where you win back covers you would otherwise lose at the door.
watch: Track ticket times for the first hour of the rush. If they climb past your normal, the bottleneck is on the line, not the floor.
follow_up: How do I staff the rush without overstaffing?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: At the busy hour, have servers offer dessert and coffee in one pass, then bring the check with the last plate instead of waiting to be asked.
why: Most slow turns are dead time after the meal, and every table you free at the peak is another party seated instead of turned away.
watch: Do it at the peak only. Rushing guests at a quiet hour costs you the regulars and gains you nothing.
follow_up: How long should a table take at our peak?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Pick one add on for each part of the menu and have every server offer it by name, such as a side with mains or a pastry with coffee.
why: One specific suggestion lifts the check without slowing service, where a vague question like anything else gets a no.
example: A $6 add on taken by 1 in 4 guests across 400 covers a week is $600 a week.
watch: Count how many get added each shift for 2 weeks. If it stays under 1 in 10, change the item, not the script.
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Raise prices in small steps on a few items at a time, starting with the dishes people order for what they are, not for the price.
why: Small regular rises keep pace with costs without the shock of one big jump that regulars notice and talk about.
example: $1 more on a dish that sells 200 a week is $200 a week, about $10,400 over a year.
watch: Watch how many of each changed item sell for 4 weeks. If one drops sharply, that dish was carrying its price, so hold it there.
follow_up: Which dishes should I raise first?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Cost your 10 best sellers to the cent this week, ingredient by ingredient, and reprice or re-portion any that run well over 30% of the menu price.
why: Most full service rooms keep food cost near 28 to 35% of sales, and your best sellers are where a few points of margin move the most money.
example: Cutting a $4 plate cost by 40 cents on a dish that sells 150 a week saves $60 a week.
watch: Recost every quarter or whenever a supplier price moves, because a dish costed last year is a guess today.
follow_up: What should my food cost be?
basis_note: Seed tactic written in house; to be checked against the researched set.

move: Build each shift to the hour you expect to be busy: stagger start times so people arrive as the rush builds and cut the first person once it falls.
why: Labor is usually your biggest cost after food, and staggered shifts put the hours where the covers are instead of across the whole day.
watch: Compare labor to sales for each shift, not each week. A shift whose labor runs well over 35% of its own sales is staffed for a different day.
follow_up: How many people should I put on for the rush?

move: Send every booking a confirmation text the day before that asks guests to reply if plans changed, and release unconfirmed tables to walk ins.
why: An empty reserved table at the peak is the most expensive seat in the room, and a reminder turns many quiet no shows into early cancellations.
watch: Track no shows by day for a month. If one night stays high, ask for a card on file for large parties that night only.
follow_up: Should I take deposits for big tables?

move: Make it a house habit to greet regulars by name and remember their usual, and note it somewhere the whole team can see.
why: Regulars carry the slow days, and being known is the main reason people pick the same place again over a cheaper one.
watch: Ask the team each week who the new regulars are. If nobody can name one, the habit has slipped.
follow_up: Should I start a loyalty card?
